articles.headline: Two Amateur Astronomers Discover Exoplanets Using OpenAI's Codex and Astra
articles.body: Two amateur astronomers leveraged OpenAI's Codex (a code generation model) and Astra (an AI tool for astronomical analysis) to identify potential exoplanets hidden within publicly available data from NASA's Kepler and TESS space telescopes. Rather than requiring professional equipment or institutional access, they tapped into existing NASA datasets that contain thousands of observations, using AI to process and analyze patterns that human researchers might miss or take significantly longer to identify. Codex allowed them to write complex data analysis scripts rapidly, while Astra provided specialized capabilities for detecting the subtle brightness dips that indicate an exoplanet passing in front of its host star. This represents a significant democratization of astronomical discovery — traditionally a field dominated by well-funded research institutions and professional observatories. By combining freely available space telescope data with accessible AI tools, amateur astronomers can now participate in genuine scientific discovery and contribute to the catalog of known exoplanets. The implications extend beyond astronomy: this model demonstrates how AI can lower barriers to entry across scientific fields, enabling citizen scientists and independent researchers to make meaningful contributions that might otherwise require years of training or institutional resources.

Instead of forcing developers to load all available tools into an agent's context window—which consumes tokens and increases latency—Tool Retrieval lets agents dynamically fetch only the specific tools they need for a given task. This means you can now give Gemini agents access to hundreds of tools while using significantly fewer tokens per request. The feature addresses a real pain point in agentic AI: as tool libraries grow, traditional approaches become expensive and slow. With Tool Retrieval, the system intelligently identifies which tools are relevant to a user's request and retrieves only those, reducing bloat and cost. This is particularly valuable for entrepreneurs building production AI agents that need broad capability sets. The technology is available now in preview on the Gemini API, allowing developers to test and integrate it into their existing applications. Google hasn't released specific benchmark numbers comparing token savings, but the efficiency gains are expected to be substantial for large tool libraries. This positions Gemini as a more practical choice for enterprise agentic applications where cost-per-inference matters.

articles.body: A new workflow combining NVIDIA's Isaac Lab simulation platform with Newton physics engine enables robots to train on obstacle avoidance in simulation and deploy directly to real hardware with high fidelity transfer. The approach addresses the persistent sim2real gap — the challenge of translating behaviors learned in perfect digital environments to unpredictable physical robots. By leveraging Isaac Lab's high-fidelity simulation capabilities and Newton's realistic physics modeling, researchers can train obstacle avoidance policies that generalize effectively to real-world conditions without extensive real-world data collection or retraining. The workflow demonstrates that robots trained entirely in simulation can navigate complex environments with moving obstacles, adapt to unseen scenarios, and maintain stable performance on actual hardware. This matters because traditional robotics requires expensive hardware time and extensive trial-and-error; this approach compresses that timeline significantly. The method is particularly valuable for autonomous systems that need to react in real-time to dynamic environments — delivery robots, warehouse automation, and mobile manipulation platforms all benefit from reliable obstacle detection and avoidance trained at zero real-world cost.

articles.hook: Robots just got way better at grabbing exactly what they need.
articles.headline: RoboTrack brings precise point tracking to real-world robot manipulation
articles.body: RoboTrack is a new point-tracking system designed to give robots the ability to precisely track and manipulate specific points on objects in real-world environments. Unlike previous approaches that relied on dense optical flow or generic feature matching, RoboTrack enables robots to follow and interact with precise spatial coordinates across video frames, translating visual tracking into actionable manipulation commands. The system works by allowing robots to identify a specific point on an object (like a corner of a box, a handle, or a surface feature) and then maintain tracking of that point as the object moves or rotates, enabling more accurate grasping, pushing, and placement tasks. This addresses a critical bottleneck in robotic manipulation: most existing systems struggle with real-world variability, lighting changes, and occlusions that occur during actual manipulation tasks. RoboTrack appears to handle these challenges by using learned representations that generalize across different objects and environments rather than relying on hand-crafted features. The capability could significantly improve pick-and-place operations, assembly tasks, and other manipulation workflows that require sub-centimeter precision. This work bridges the gap between computer vision research and practical robotics, making it relevant for manufacturers, logistics companies, and any operation using collaborative or autonomous robots for object handling.
examples: Track a specific point on a package and guide a robot arm to grasp it consistently, even as the package shifts position.
Enable a robot to follow a seam or edge on an object through multiple manipulation steps without losing precision.
Teach a robot to manipulate deformable objects by tracking key points that change shape during handling.

articles.hook: OpenAI and Cisco just made Linux security actually simple.
articles.headline: OpenAI and Cisco Launch Shirudo: Open-Source Runtime Patches Systems Without Downtime
articles.body: OpenAI and Cisco have introduced Shirudo, an open-source runtime for Linux that allows teams to deploy security patches and updates to running systems without taking them offline. The tool addresses a critical pain point for DevOps and infrastructure teams: the traditional patch-and-restart cycle that can cause service interruptions, lost revenue, and customer frustration. Shirudo enables live patching, meaning security updates can be applied to kernel and system components while applications continue running uninterrupted. This is particularly valuable for mission-critical systems like payment processors, cloud infrastructure, databases, and enterprise servers that cannot afford downtime. The runtime works by injecting patches directly into running processes, eliminating the need for scheduled maintenance windows. This approach reduces vulnerability exposure windows — the dangerous period between when a patch is released and when it's actually deployed — from hours or days down to minutes. For teams managing large fleets of servers, Shirudo can mean the difference between rapid response to zero-day vulnerabilities and risky delays waiting for maintenance schedules. The open-source nature means enterprises can audit the code, integrate it into their existing infrastructure, and avoid vendor lock-in. Shirudo represents a significant shift in how modern infrastructure teams can balance security velocity with uptime requirements.

Deploy fixes to running applications without triggering cascading restarts across your entire infrastructure.

articles.hook: Building AI agents that actually work is harder than it looks.
articles.headline: HuggingFace reveals how to build and evaluate agentic AI systems properly
articles.body: HuggingFace has published a comprehensive guide on building and maintaining agentic evaluation frameworks — the systematic approach to testing whether AI agents perform reliably in real-world scenarios. As AI agents become more complex, moving beyond simple chatbots to systems that can take multiple steps, make decisions, and interact with external tools, the need for robust evaluation has become critical. The guide covers the entire lifecycle: defining what success looks like for your specific agent, creating realistic test scenarios, measuring performance across different conditions, and continuously monitoring agent behavior in production. This addresses a real pain point in the AI builder community — most evaluation frameworks were designed for static language models, not for agents that need to plan, iterate, and adapt. The core challenge is that traditional metrics like BLEU scores or accuracy don't capture whether an agent actually accomplishes its goal or fails gracefully when it encounters problems. HuggingFace breaks down practical approaches including trace-based evaluation (analyzing the full decision path), outcome-based metrics (did the agent complete the task?), and human-in-the-loop validation for high-stakes applications. The framework emphasizes maintaining evaluation consistency as agents evolve and new tools get added to their toolkit, since agent behavior can be surprisingly brittle — small changes can cause unexpected failures.
examples: Create test scenarios where agents must sequence multiple API calls correctly to solve a customer support problem.
Track whether an agent asks clarifying questions when instructions are ambiguous versus making incorrect assumptions.
Measure how agents handle failures — do they retry intelligently or loop endlessly wasting tokens and time?

articles.hook: Walter Isaacson just revealed what AI can't steal from you.
articles.headline: Walter Isaacson: History's greatest innovators show AI needs human creativity
articles.body: Walter Isaacson, the renowned biographer of Steve Jobs, Leonardo da Vinci, and Elon Musk, joined Google to discuss how the innovators he's studied throughout his career can teach us to thrive in the AI age. Isaacson argues that while AI excels at processing information and finding patterns, the qualities that made history's greatest creators legendary—curiosity, judgment, and the ability to connect disparate ideas—remain uniquely human strengths. The core insight: as AI commoditizes routine cognitive work, the premium on human creativity and judgment actually increases rather than decreases. Isaacson points to da Vinci's insatiable curiosity across disciplines, Jobs' obsession with the intersection of technology and liberal arts, and Musk's ability to imagine possibilities others dismiss as impossible. These aren't skills AI replicates; they're the foundation for directing and elevating what AI can do. For entrepreneurs building with AI, the message is clear—the future belongs to those who can combine AI's computational power with distinctly human judgment about what problems matter and why.
examples: Combine AI's ability to generate 100 marketing angles with human judgment to pick the ones that actually resonate with your audience's real emotions.
Use AI to analyze historical data and find patterns, then apply human creativity to imagine new business models competitors haven't thought of yet.
Let AI handle the heavy lifting of content production, then apply your unique perspective and storytelling to make it something people actually care about.
articles.build: Consultants are charging $5K-$15K per project to help founders identify which human skills their business needs to protect and amplify as they automate with AI. Executive coaches are running 6-week sprints ($2K-$8K per person) teaching teams how to cultivate curiosity and creative thinking alongside AI tools. Some agencies are building retainers ($3K-$10K/month) for founders who want monthly guidance on where to apply human judgment versus automation in their workflows.

articles.hook: Google just made Gemini work on phones everyone actually owns.
articles.headline: Google expands Gemini app to lower-memory Android devices with Live and image creation
articles.body: Google has expanded access to its Gemini app to lower-memory Android devices, removing a previous barrier that limited the AI assistant to phones with higher specs. The update enables users on budget and mid-range Android phones to access Gemini Live—the real-time conversational feature that lets users talk naturally with the AI—as well as custom image generation capabilities. Previously, Gemini's most powerful features were restricted to flagship devices with more RAM and processing power, leaving millions of Android users unable to experience the full functionality. This expansion matters because it democratizes access to AI tools across a much larger addressable market; Android dominates global smartphone share, and most users globally own mid-range or lower-spec devices rather than premium flagships. The move suggests Google is optimizing Gemini's performance and reducing computational overhead, making the app leaner and faster on constrained hardware. For entrepreneurs building AI-powered services or consulting on AI tool adoption, this expands the total addressable market—businesses can now pitch Gemini solutions to teams and clients with any Android phone, not just premium device owners. Download and installation are available immediately through the Google Play Store.
examples: Open Gemini Live on a budget Android phone and have a natural voice conversation about your business problem.
Generate custom images directly in the Gemini app to create social media content without leaving your phone.
Use Gemini on your older Android device to get real-time AI assistance while traveling or working in the field.
